2) House property bearing 367 comprising of ground floor chawl, situated at Lane No. 55,
Chickenghar within Kalyan Dombivali Municipal Corporation (KDMC) is owned by the Plaintiff.
Room No.1 divided into three rooms admeasuring 300 sq. ft. in house No.367 are the 'suit premises'.
Father of Defendant Nos. 1 to 3-late Chatrabhuj Barot was inducted as monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises on monthly rent of Rs.25/-.

It is alleged by Plaintiff that Defendant No.1- Kirit Kumar Chatrabhuj Barot was residing in the suit premises and Defendant No.2-Bakul Chatrabhuj Barot has shifted alongwith his family in his owned house at
Thakkar Co-op. Housing Society Ltd.

It is further alleged that Defendant No.3 has been residing with Defendant No.2 in the house of Defendant No.2 since 1996- 1997 and thereafter shifted to his own house at Mohan Park, Khadak Pada, Kalyan (W).
This is how Plaintiff claimed that Defendant No.1 alone resides in the suit premises alongwith his family.

Plaintiff instituted R.C.S. No.45 of 2007 in the Court of C.J.J.D.,
Kalyan on 23 January 2007 alleging that Defendant No.1 erected permanent structure of kitchen platform and 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx bathroom inside the suit premises, that he chiseled the wall between two rooms and installed permanent marble temple thereby endangering the wall of the suit premises.
Plaintiff therefore claimed that Defendant No.1 caused damage to the suit premises.
It was further alleged in the Plaint that Defendant No.1 is an auto rickshaw driver and was illegally parking his auto rickshaw in the open space belonging to the Plaintiff.
That Defendant Nos.2 and 3 are taxi drivers, who also parked their taxis in Plaintiff's property during nighttime.
That the local hooligans were misusing the parked vehicles and creating nuisance to Plaintiff, his family members and neighbouring occupiers.

It was further alleged that the wife of Defendant No.1- Jayashri K. Barot was conducting private classes in the suit premises without the consent of the landlord and that the students attending her tuitions were creating nuisance for Plaintiff and neighbouring occupiers by their various acts such as throwing stones at mango tree, using common toilet, occupying common spaces, etc.

Lastly, Plaintiff also claimed that he had decided to demolish the house structure in which the suit premises are located and to construct a new building and had expressed willingness to provide the same area in the new building to the Defendant No.1 by charging mere construction cost, on ownership basis.

That Defendant No.1 accordingly executed consent letter dated 4 January 2006 and accordingly Plaintiff got plans sanctioned for construction of new building from KDMC and accordingly commenced construction of the building since May-2006.

However, despite the developer 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx engaged by the Plaintiff repeatedly calling upon Defendant No.1 to select flat in the new building Defendant No.1 refused to co- operate.
Accordingly, Plaintiff also sought recovery of possession of the suit premises for demolition and construction of new building.
The Suit was resisted by Defendants by filing their written statement contesting the claim of the Plaintiff in the Suit.
Defendants denied the allegations of permanent construction, cause of damage to the suit premises, cause of nuisance /annoyance to Plaintiff/ neighbouring occupants.
So far as consent letter dated 4 January 2006 is concerned, Defendants contended that signature of Defendant No.1 was obtained on blank paper for preparation of false consent letter.
That Plaintiff unauthorisedly secured development permission from Municipal Corporation without informing Defendants or other tenants.
Defendants therefore denied that Plaintiff was entitled to secure possession of the suit premises for construction of new building in accordance with the said plans.

6) Mr. Naphade, the learned counsel appearing for the Revision Applicants would submit that the Trial and the Appellate Courts have grossly erred in decreeing the Suit of Plaintiffs.

That so far as the ground of causing damage to suit premises by reason of installation of mandir is concerned,
Plaintiff did not produce any evidence to prove the act of chiseling of walls for mounting of the temple.

That even if it is assumed that the temple has indeed been mounted on the wall separating kitchen and hall, there is absolutely no evidence on record to even remotely suggest that such an act resulted in any destruction or injury to the suit premises.
He would submit that the entire burden of proving damage or injury to the suit premises was on the Plaintiff, who has miserably failed to discharge the same.

It appears from the findings recorded by the Trial Court in para-12 of its judgment that construction of kitchen platform, enclosed bathroom and marble temple is essentially considered by the Trial Court for answering Issue No.1 relating to permanent construction in the Plaintiff's favour.
The Trial Court did not have any factual material before it except the oral evidence of Plaintiff's constituted attorney and of Defendant No.1.
No Court Commissioner was appointed to ascertain the exact factual situation at the suit premises.

Merely on the basis of oral evidence of Defendant No.1, where he stated in his cross-examination that he did not have knowledge about existence of kitchen platform or enclosed bathroom in the suit premises,
the Trial Court considered the age of Defendant No.1 as on 6 September 2011 when he filed Affidavit of evidence and ascertained his age as 18 years in 1978 when his father was inducted as a tenant.

The Trial Court accordingly drew adverse inference against Defendant No.1 by disbelieving his statement about lack of knowledge about existence of kitchen platform or enclosed bathroom in the suit premises.
On this material alone, the Trial Court proceeded to hold that Defendants carried out permanent construction in the suit premises without landlord's consent.

So far as the ground of change of user in Issue No.2 is 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx concerned, the same is accepted on the ground that the wife of Defendant No.1 conducted tuitions in the suit premises.

18) The Appellate Court however committed a blatant error in reversing the findings of the Trial Court on the issue of nuisance and annoyance.
As observed above, the Trial Court had rejected the ground of nuisance/annoyance holding that no other tenants/neighbours were examined to prove cause of nuisance.
In absence of any cross-examination by the Plaintiff, the Appellate Court erroneously reversed the said finding of the Trial Court.

Though it is true that the Appellate Court can exercise powers under Order XLI Rules 32 and 33 of the Code to reverse finding of the Trial Court recorded in favour of Defendant in an Appeal filed by the Defendant, the Appellate Court has nowhere made it clear that it was exercising any particular power under the Code for doing so.
In fact, the Appellate Court was not even conscious of the fact that it was reversing the finding of the Trial Court on the issue of nuisance/annoyance.
The Appellate Court has recorded its finding on Issue No.6 in paragraphs-22 and 23 of its judgment on the issue of nuisance/annoyance as if the said ground was accepted by the Trial Court as well.
The Appellate Court has nowhere recorded in its finding that the Trial Court had erred in rejecting the ground of nuisance/annoyance.
Thus, the findings of the 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx Appellate Court on the issue of nuisance/annoyance clearly suffers from non-application of mind.

No doubt it is true that 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx in a given case,
Plaintiff-landlord himself can be adjoining or neighbouring occupier and therefore if the Plaintiff-landlord suffers the act of nuisance/annoyance, he can very well maintain a suit under Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act and in such case, it is not necessary for the Plaintiff-landlord to additionally prove acts of nuisance/annoyance to any other neighbouring occupier.
However, in a case where Plaintiff himself is not a neighbouring occupier, it is incumbent for the Plaintiff to examine a neighbouring occupier who actually suffers the act of tenant amounting to nuisance/annoyance.
In the present case, not even a single neighbouring occupier is examined by the Plaintiff.
Plaintiff himself did not step into the witness box and evidence is led by his constituted attorney.
It has come in evidence that Plaintiff is residing at Mumbai and does not reside in the neighbourhood of the suit premises.
Plaintiff is thus not neighbouring occupier.
Therefore, the Appellate Court has erred in accepting the ground under Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act.
The findings recorded by the Appellate Court with regard to the ground of nuisance/annoyance are thus unsustainable and liable to be set aside.

18) The Appellate Court however committed a blatant error in reversing the findings of the Trial Court on the issue of nuisance and annoyance.

the Appellate Court committed a fundamental error in not appreciating the fact that the Plaintiff was residing at Mumbai and not a neighbouring occupier.
It would be apposite to reproduce provisions of Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act:

9 20) Thus, for seeking recovery of the suit premises under Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act, what needs to be proved is conduct of the tenant which has caused nuisance/annoyance to the 'adjoining or neighbouring occupier'.
No doubt it is true that 12 December 2024 Megha 2_cra_53_2023_fc.docx in a given case,
Plaintiff-landlord himself can be adjoining or neighbouring occupier and therefore if the Plaintiff-landlord suffers the act of nuisance/annoyance, he can very well maintain a suit under Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act and in such case, it is not necessary for the Plaintiff-landlord to additionally prove acts of nuisance/annoyance to any other neighbouring occupier.
However, in a case where Plaintiff himself is not a neighbouring occupier, it is incumbent for the Plaintiff to examine a neighbouring occupier who actually suffers the act of tenant amounting to nuisance/annoyance.
In the present case, not even a single neighbouring occupier is examined by the Plaintiff.
Plaintiff himself did not step into the witness box and evidence is led by his constituted attorney.
It has come in evidence that Plaintiff is residing at Mumbai and does not reside in the neighbourhood of the suit premises.
Plaintiff is thus not neighbouring occupier.
Therefore, the Appellate Court has erred in accepting the ground under Section 16(1)(c) of the MRC Act.
The findings recorded by the Appellate Court with regard to the ground of nuisance/annoyance are thus unsustainable and liable to be set aside.
